anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently chooses a highly inefficient execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to excessive I/O, CPU, or memory demand per statement.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions fight for hot buffer-cache pages and the latches that protect them, producing long page-latch waits and spin CPU with limited throughput gain.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client/server communication paths or connection slots are saturated, causing connection delays, socket-level back-pressure, and session wait events on client reads or writes.

When all three root causes strike together, the workload experiences a multilayer slowdown: (1) bad plans drive up logical and physical I/O, inflating demand on the buffer pool; (2) the resulting surge in page pins and dirty-page churn amplifies latch contention and buffer busy waits; (3) the elongated execution and commit times hold server processes and network sockets open longer, swelling session counts and outbound data queues. Symptoms may include erratic plan flips accompanied by sudden spikes in page-latch and buffer-busy waits, CPU saturation from spin loops, growing numbers of connections in authentication or established-idle states, and cascading client time-outs. Performance views may show high variance in execution plans, hot-page contention centred on index roots or sequencing tables, and network retransmissions or listener backlog exhaustion, making it hard to attribute latency to a single tier.

Causally, a poor plan that scans large data ranges floods the buffer pool, evicting useful pages and forcing frequent page replacement. This heightens latch pressure as many sessions attempt to pin or dirty the same root and leaf pages. The prolonged critical-section holds extend statement duration, so each session monopolizes its backend thread and TCP socket for longer, pushing the connection pool and listener toward saturation. Conversely, network slowdowns or connection-establishment delays can elongate transaction lifetimes, aggravating buffer residency pressure and increasing the window during which latch contention manifests. The intertwined feedback loop means that relieving only one layer often yields limited benefit; comprehensive remediation must address plan stability, buffer/latch hot spots, and network or connection scaling parameters in concert.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
